And they recognize it's going to be very challenging, and they're very dedicated to having that happen. In rolling out AI and having the incredible beneficial outcomes, whether that's the Waymo self-driving, whether that's gene editing, whether that's curing cancer. You know, 10, 20 years from now, it's very likely we'll have pretty abundant energy. We will have amazing health outcomes. I mean, so much positive outcome from the AI infusion into science. And I would say Anthropic is very serious about helping us manage or avoid most of the downside.

SK: And how have you all pulled that off in closed doors? I've been in some of those closed doors where people are genuinely afraid, more than 10% chance that this could be an existential threat to humanity. It does seem that Anthropic somehow is proving to be very responsible, or that's what it appears to be, and at the same time, moving very fast, hyperspeed. It feels like almost every few weeks there's something new, and it's very tangible in what it might do for work. How are you all balancing that at Anthropic instead of just saying "go, go, go"?

RH: You know, I think all of the big models are improving rapidly. You're probably going to see them go -- certain ones will lead in certain areas over time. And, you know, frankly, it's good for the country if we have three really successful models to choose from. And then how do they balance it? You know, case by case. So I think each one I have to see, you know, how accelerated is learning? How powerful is it? What are the downside scenarios? What are the new possibilities it can do? SK: I'm curious about Anthropic itself. I had a chance to visit there a couple of weeks ago. I take pride that Khan Academy, we’re super nimble and innovating. And we're obviously trying to leverage AI for social good as much as possible. When I visited there, I tangibly felt that they were pioneering completely new ways of running an organization, new ways of developing product. I think it was something like Cowork -- what was it, a week or two? That it was essentially built primarily by the AI itself. What will an organization look like in the future? I think you'll have a pretty good crystal ball there.

RH: Yeah, I don't know that most companies will come to look like Anthropic. I think it really depends on your industry. If you happen to be a pure software company, then it might be relevant for that class of company. But broadly across the economy, I think everyone is figuring out -- you know, it's a bigger version of the internet wave where all companies had to, you know, do things, and we used to talk about our AOL keyword and crazy stuff like that, which was the phasing in. This is a lot bigger and more intense, but it's sort of a larger version of that same thing, which is all companies around the world, organizations, governments, militaries, are scrambling to figure out, you know, how to use AI well.

SK: I guess related to that -- people are talking about it with software engineering, people are talking about call centers. I have a friend -- one of his startups has a call center in the Philippines. They're going to lay off 80%. That's 7% of that country's GDP. How are you thinking about jobs? Just as a thinker, how is Anthropic thinking about it?

RH: Well, look, if you look over the last 200 years, there have been a bunch of dislocations, but they, you know, happened slowly and over one part of the economy. And so the danger is, you know, are there multiple -- that happen in multiple fields? If these happen slowly, then people are able to find other roles. So it depends on how fast this all comes. And again, I would say the biggest uncertainty for everybody is how fast is the AI getting better and how fast will it be getting better going forward? And then that changes your views and assumptions.

So let’s look at self-driving cars. I mean, we thought 20 years ago it was going to be pretty fast. And it's 20 years later from when it started in 2007, and the DARPA Grand Challenge -- we’re at what, 0.1% of all miles, maybe 0.001%? I mean, it's really pretty tiny. 20 years later. So these things take a long time to actually mature and diffuse. Another example is Geoffrey Hinton won the Nobel Prize for his work on neural nets and really the father of AI. And in 2016, so ten years ago, he said, "Stop training radiologists now, because in five years, 2021, there would be no need for them." So what's happened instead is as radiology got AI-boosted, the cost came down, [and] you can walk into an MRI center in the US for $300 and get an MRI now. And so docs started ordering them more and using them more, and insurance covered them more. And so the number of scans has gone way up. And guess what? We have a shortage in radiologists. We have 35,000. We need about 40,000. Wages have climbed to close to $500,000 a year. So even the best-intentioned people in the field can prophesy disaster in radiology and have it be not accurate. And it's just a timing thing because in 20 years, I'm confident Hinton will be right. So just think, there's two examples there, which is a lot of the stuff may not happen right away, but it's still probably going to happen in a long time, 20 years. Some of it might happen in a short time. So you want to be ready for it.

SK: And that makes sense. Although something does feel different about this time. And all the people leading these AI labs are talking about not 20 years, they're talking about next year, they're talking about two years. You're going to have a data center of superintelligent geniuses that can do our work. Do you think they're wrong or do you think it's a probability? And even if it’s a 10% chance that they’re right, are you worried that this can lead to political polarization? What happened in globalization can now happen, what happened in 30 years could happen in two or three. Is that not a concern, or should we start doing something about that?
RH: If the AI really gets incredible in a very short amount of time, like starts writing itself and self-improving all of that --
SK: Isn't it writing 90% of itself right now?

RH: You know, again, lines of code is a tricky measure. You know, when it's invented a new type of learning, so there's, you know, reinforcement learning, when it invents something completely new, then you can say that. But there are cases where it's pretty fast. And so I think it's important to say we should be ready. Here's the thing. We talk a bunch about unemployment, what it will do. Every other time we’ve had big unemployment, it's been a recession, and so the stock market's down and government tax revenues are down. This time, if AI is successful in the way we think it will, I think we're going to see high productivity, high GDP growth, high stock market and high unemployment. So we'll have money to do things. And so think of it like the Alaska Fund, which is oil, or the Norwegian sovereign fund. We need some ideas like that. What are we going to do with all these huge tax revenues that are going to be able to come in with big growth? And if we’ve got a fund that is for the benefit of all citizens, then we may in fact be able to have a path to a glorious and harmonious society. And I don't mean, you know, UBI, that's got a bad taint to it, but it's a partial sharing of the rewards, which is again, what happened with the Alaska Fund and in the Norwegian fund.
SK: Makes sense. Reed Hastings, thank you so much. And thanks, everyone. Accelerating possibilities.
(Applause)

When a community wants to build a bridge or transit system, housing, sustainable infrastructure -- where does the money come from? Money ultimately decides what gets built. Money decides what survives. Money decides what future becomes possible. So change where money goes and who controls it -- then you change what becomes possible.

I'm Trinity Tran, I lead efforts to build public banks in California and beyond. Most of the time, our cities don’t have the money upfront to be able to pay for a project like a bridge or housing. And so they will issue a bond, which is essentially a long-term loan, provided [and] structured by Wall Street banks. A loan is money that is provided upfront and paid back over time with interest. Wall Street banks -- private lenders -- end up tacking on fees to structure and sell those bonds. Then the reality is that our local governments are not only paying for the cost of the project, but decades of interest on top of that. So for every dollar that we're borrowing, we're paying another dollar in interest over time, sometimes more. And that's all money that's going out the door to private lenders. We're paying hundreds of millions of dollars in the city of Los Angeles. At the state level, in California, we’re paying $4 billion in interest annually. That's money flowing out of our communities rather than being invested locally. Private banks are owned by shareholders. They're investing in areas that make them a lot of money, and not necessarily what’s in the best interest of our communities. Public banking asks a different question: how do we do more with the dollars that our communities generate without raising taxes, but by lowering the cost of financing itself?

A public bank is a bank owned by the people through their local government, either city or region or state. Every time you buy something, like a cup of coffee, a portion of that tax will go to your city and your state. So we're using the money that we already generate that belongs to us. They don't have shareholders to pay. So as loans are repaid, it comes back into a public bank. Its mission is to support the local economic development of the community it serves. That would be designed at a local level. So the law that we created -- the California Public Banking Act -- created the legal framework for cities and municipalities to be able to form their own banks. And so the mission of the bank, the mandates, the lending priorities, the investment priorities, the capitalization strategies, all the details of how this is going to work is going to be defined at a local level.

There are 900 public banks globally with nearly $50 trillion in assets. In Germany, a network of 400 municipal banks was able to support the country's renewable energy transition. In the United States, we have a successful model to emulate. The Bank of North Dakota is a 100-year-old public bank founded in 1919. It was started by socialist farmers who were being gouged by out-of-state New York bankers. During the Great Depression, nearly 200,000 farms were being foreclosed on. Because the state of North Dakota had a public bank, it was able to step in and buy the farms and lend it back to the families for a dollar. Once the families were able to stabilize, they sold it back at a price they could afford. For the last century, it has supported local economic development, supported small businesses, infrastructure while still returning very healthy return on equity, 15 to 18 percent. That means it's returning hundreds of millions of dollars back into the general fund year after year. So that's an example of how a public bank is able to step in and support and strengthen the community without focusing on just purely profit.

Los Angeles just dealt with a devastating wildfire. So if we had a public bank, it would have been able to step in to offer immediate, low-cost loans. It's able to be immediately responsive to the needs of the community without having to wait for federal aid, which can be unstable. We're moving towards building a system that mobilizes public revenue to support our public priorities. We've seen such an incredible amount of progress in such a short time, because even without a complex understanding of finance and banking, when you start explaining public banking, it makes sense on a logical, intuitive level. Multiple cities and states are working towards it. We have the ability to create a new system. This isn't a pie-in-the-sky idea. This is a model that works for the people, our communities and our environment.
zh: 当一个社区想要建造 桥梁或交通系统、住房， 可持续基础设施时—— 资金来自哪里？ 资金最终决定什么能建成。 资金决定什么存活。 资金决定哪种未来成为可能。 因此，改变资金的去向和主宰的人—— 这样你就能改变成为可能的事情。

我是特里妮蒂·陈， 我领导加利福尼亚及以外地区 建立公共银行的工作。 通常情况下，我们的城市没有预付款 来支付桥梁或住房等项目的费用。 因此，他们将发行债券， 本质上是长期贷款， 由华尔街银行设计并提供。 贷款是预先提供并逐步偿还利息的资金， 华尔街银行——私人贷款机构—— 最终收取额外费用 以设计和发行这些债券。 那么现实情况是，我们的地方政府 不仅要支付项目成本， 还要支付数十年的利息。 因此，对于我们借来的每一美元， 随着时间推移， 还要再支付另一美元的利息， 有时甚至更多。 而这些都是流向私人贷款机构的钱。 我们支付数十亿美元 在洛杉矶城市。 在州一级，在加州， 我们每年要支付 40 亿美元的利息。 这是从我们的社区流出的资金 而不是投资于当地。 私人银行归股东所有。 他们投资于能为他们赚很多钱的领域， 但不一定符合我们社区的最大利益。 公共银行提出了另一个问题： 我们如何利用社区产生的资金 做更多的事情 在不增加税收 而是降低资金成本的情况下？

公共银行是人民通过地方政府 （城市、地区或州）拥有的银行。 每次你买东西，比如一杯咖啡， 一部分税款将流向你的城市和州。 因此，我们正在使用 自己赚到的、属于我们的钱。 他们没有股东需要付款。 因此，在偿还贷款时， 它会归还给公共银行。 其使命是支持 所服务社区的当地经济发展。 这将由地方层面来设计。 因此，我们制定了法律—— 《加州公共银行法》—— 为城市和市镇建立了 法律责任框架 使其组建自己的银行。 因此，银行的使命、 授权、贷款优先事项、 投资重点、资本化策略， 以及其运作方式的所有细节 都将由地方层面确定。

全球有 900 家公共银行， 拥有近 50 万亿美元的资产。 在德国，由 400 家市政银行 组成的网络 能够支持该国的可再生能源转型。 在美国，我们有 一个成功的模式可以效仿。 北达科他银行 是一家拥有 100 年历史的公共银行， 成立于 1919 年。 它由被外州纽约银行家所盘剥的 社会主义农民发起。 在大萧条期间， 近 20 万家农场面临 被强制拍卖的局面。 由于北达科他州有一家公共银行， 它得以介入并购买农场， 然后以一美元的价格将其借还给家庭。 一旦这些家庭能够稳定下来， 他们就会以自己负担 得起的价格将其卖回。 上个世纪， 它支持了当地经济发展， 支持了小型企业和基础设施 同时仍然恢复了非常可观的股本回报率， 15 ％至 18 ％。 这意味着它年复一年地 向普通基金返还数亿美元。 因此，这是一个例子， 说明公共银行如何支持 并加强社区建设， 在不单纯追求利润的情况下。

洛杉矶刚刚发生了一场毁灭性的野火 如果我们有公共银行 它将能够介入 并立即提供低成本贷款。 它能够立即响应社区的需求 而不必等待可能不稳定的 联邦援助。 我们正在努力建立一个体系， 能调动公共收入 以支持我们的公共优先事项。 我们在如此短的时间内看到了 如此惊人的进步， 因为即使对金融和银行没有复杂的了解， 当你开始解释公共银行时， 从逻辑和直观的层面来看也是有道理的。 多个城市和州正在朝这一目标努力。 我们有能力创建一个新体系。 这不是一个天上掉馅饼的想法。 这种模式对人们， 社区和我们的环境都有效。

en: I want to be long-winded and unclear. It's not a common opening line. Most people won't tell us when they're going to be long-winded, but we know. We can tell pretty quickly if someone’s going to get to the point or if we are in for a long and painful conversation. And this is especially true at work. Every year, poor communication costs businesses hundreds of billions of dollars in lost productivity. And I have to confess, [in] the early part of my career, I was responsible for at least some of that. But I'm not alone.

Hands up if you work with someone who is long winded or unclear. That's a lot of hands. Now I’m sure we are all thinking about people outside this room, right? Except for those of you pointing at each other. But what would happen if we asked the people outside this room? They might be thinking about us. And while our goal is to be clear and concise, do we really know how?

Every time we communicate, we have an opportunity to create clarity or confusion. And clarity begins from the very first minute. If you get the first minute right, you set your conversation up for success. Get it wrong [and] your conversations will be longer, less effective and more frustrating.

Now on the off chance we could all use a little more clarity, I'm going to share a tip with you today. A tip that will help each of you improve the success of your communication at work. A tip that has been tested by more than 75,000 people around the world. And a tip that will help each of you get the first minute right. And here it is. There are three things we must include at the start of our work messages. And those three things begin with T, I and P. It's a TIP.

Now the first part of the tip is the T, and T stands for topic. Every conversation at work needs a clear topic. When the topic is clear, everyone knows what we're talking about. Everyone's in sync. Everybody understands. Unfortunately, reality isn't always like this, is it? How often are you in a conversation and you find yourself thinking, what are you talking about?
(Laughter)
That happens when the topic is not clear. Now usually the consequences are pretty minor -- a little bit of wasted time, some minor frustration -- but sometimes, the consequences are more significant.

In 2006, I was part of an engineering team writing a bid -- a proposal -- that was worth a lot of money to our company. And a couple of days before the big meeting, my boss came up to me and said, "Hey, Chris, I need you to change the meeting from Tuesday to Thursday." So off I went and I changed the meeting. I typed an email, sent it to the client saying, "Something’s come up, we've got to change." And about a minute after I hit send, my phone rings. It's my boss. He had one question: "Why did you change the meeting?" You see, he was talking about our one-to-one, and I was thinking about the client meeting. The lack of a clear topic meant he and I were thinking about two very different things. Now that might be the single biggest contribution I’ve made to the cost of bad communication, but it also marks the moment at which I began to be interested in improving how we communicate at work.

So all our messages have to begin with a clear topic. But how? How do we do this? It's really easy. Start your message with one sentence that names the topic you want to talk about, and the more specific, the better. You could say, "I'd like to talk about July sales figures." "I want to talk about Project Everest's timeline." Or "Can I talk about our one-to-one this week?" One message, one sentence that lets your audience know what the topic is. They won't be thinking, "What are you talking about?"

Now having a clear topic is a great start, but it's not enough. We need the second part of the tip, which is the I. And I stands for intent. Intent is what we want the other person to do with our message. Have you ever been in a conversation and a few minutes in thought, "Why are you telling me this?" That happens when the intent isn't clear, when the speaker hasn't told you what to do with the information that they are giving you.

Now there’s a process in our brains called selective attention, and this filters incoming information and tells you what is important and what is not. And if you don't know what to do with a message, your brain says, not important. And we stop listening. At the beginning of this talk, I told you I would give you a tip that would help improve the success of your communication at work. That told your brains what to do with this information. If I hadn't done that, I could be faced with a room full of people smiling politely while all thinking, "Why are you telling us this?" Now that is something we want to avoid at work. But there is another, and perhaps more important reason to make your intent clear.

You want to avoid frustrating the people you're talking to. I'd had a particularly bad day, and I walked into my colleague Tina's office, and I sat down with my head in my hands, and I told her how I'd messed up on an important call with a senior leader. And when I finished talking, Tina very, very helpfully said, "Oh, why don't you try this and maybe we can avoid this next time." And she was giving me all sorts of advice. The more she spoke, the more frustrated I became. I didn't want her help. And that must have been quite obvious because she just put up her hands and said, "You clearly don't want my help. So why are you here?" I said, "Tina, I'm really sorry. I just want to get this off my chest. Can I just talk for a minute?" And like a mother talking to a small child, she rolled her eyes and said, "Well, why didn't you start with that?" We need to tell our audience what to do with the information we're giving them. Tina was working hard from the moment I started talking. And all the way through, she was working hard to help me and I didn't want or need that. She was annoyed and rightly so. So when you start your message, after you've given a clear topic, tell your audience what to do with it. And again, you can do this with one line. Make your intent clear. If you have a question, say, "Can I ask you a question?" If you want someone to make a decision, say, "I'd like your help with this decision." If you want to get something off your chest, just say, "Is it OK if I vent for a minute?" If you tell your audience what to do with your message, not only will their brains pay more attention, you will avoid frustrating them. That's kind of useful.

So we've made our topic clear. We've told our audience what we intend for them to do. It's time to get down into the detail, right? Get into the message. Wrong. This is where we need the third part of the tip. The P. And P stands for point. Point is the most important part of our message. If you only had five seconds to speak, it's what you would say. And usually it's what your audience cares about the most.

When I was a kid, my dad played a game with me. If we were going on a journey, I'd go, "Dad, where are we going?" And he'd say, "Well, first, we're going to the car and then we’ll get in the car, leave the driveway, turn left onto the main street until we get to the post office, and then turn right until we go to a big yellow building." I just wanted to scream, "Where are we going?" I wanted the short version. I think he just wanted to wind me up a little bit. But fast forward a few years, I was doing the same thing at work. Someone would ask me a question, or I’d start a conversation, and I would give all the detail, step by step information. And every so often -- OK, quite often -- people would say, "Chris, just get to the point." And that's what we need. We need a point, we need a headline, something that tells us where this conversation is going.

Now, of course, there's a lot more information we could include, but that comes later. That comes after we've set up the audience to understand what the conversation is about. And we can do this quite simply, as the military likes to say, “Put the bottom line up front.” In one sentence, deliver the most important piece of information. "I want to give a refund for a late delivery." "Our project launch is going to be delayed by a month." Say the most important thing, and your audience will know where that conversation is going and they won't be thinking, "What is your point?"

Now if you start your conversation with topic, intent and point, you are starting with a clear and concise introduction, an introduction that answers the three questions we all have: What are you talking about? Why are you telling me this? And what is your point? Because here's the truth. Every time we communicate, it is an opportunity to create clarity or confusion. And topic, intent and point is clarity.

So I have a challenge for you. The next time you start a conversation at work, the next time you write a message, take a moment and think to yourself, what is my topic? What do I intend for the other person to do with this message? And what point do I want to deliver? Imagine working somewhere where everybody did this. Imagine if everyone always knew what to do with the message you gave them, or understood what it was about. How much smoother, how much easier would our jobs be? That, ladies and gentlemen, is the power of the first minute.
Thank you.
(Applause)
